---

# "Disaster is rarely as pervasive as it seems from recorded accounts" — Barbara Tuchman

## Introduction: Tuchman's Law

In the introduction to her 1978 book *A Distant Mirror*, Tuchman playfully identified a historical phenomenon which she termed "Tuchman's Law." The law states, in her words, that disaster is rarely as pervasive as it seems from recorded accounts. The fact of being on the record makes it appear continuous and ubiquitous, whereas it is more likely to have been sporadic both in time and place. Besides, persistence of the normal is usually greater than the effect of the disturbance.

Tuchman elaborated this with a vivid contemporary analogy: after absorbing the news of today, one expects to face a world consisting entirely of strikes, crimes, power failures, broken water mains, stalled trains, school shutdowns, muggers, drug addicts, neo-Nazis, and rapists. The fact is that one can come home in the evening — on a lucky day — without having encountered more than one or two of these phenomena.

She extended this into a precise formulation: "The fact of being reported multiplies the apparent extent of any deplorable development by five- to tenfold."

This deceptively simple idea opens up profound questions about the nature of historical writing, human psychology, media dynamics, and the relationship between catastrophe and everyday life. The statement has much to recommend it, but it must also be carefully scrutinised and qualified.

---

## I. The Argument in Favour: Why Tuchman's Law Rings True

### 1. The Selective Nature of Historical Records

The most fundamental support for Tuchman's claim lies in the very construction of historical records. Records are not random samples of life — they are curated, purposeful documents. Chronicles, legal records, diaries, and annals are almost always written *because* something unusual or terrible has occurred. Normal harvests, uneventful days, and quiet communities rarely generate documentation. The result is an archive inherently skewed toward crisis.

Survivorship bias is a statistical error that results from concentrating on entities that passed a selection process while overlooking those that did not. This can lead to incorrect conclusions because of incomplete data. In the historical context, it is not just individual people who "survive" into the record — it is *events*. Disasters survive into records; normalcy does not.

Large, successful organisations such as the Women's Institute, which were well organised and still have accessible archives for historians to work from, are studied more than smaller charitable organisations, even though these may have done a great deal of work. The same logic applies to disasters: catastrophic events leave dramatic traces — chronicles, laments, legal adjustments — while the steady continuity of life leaves almost none.

### 2. The Black Death: A Tuchman Case Study

Tuchman developed her "Law" in the context of writing about the calamitous 14th century, dominated by the Black Death. Her point can be tested directly against the evidence.

The Black Death epidemic of *Yersinia pestis* (1347–50 CE) killed about half the population of England, and many historical changes have been ascribed to it. But we still know surprisingly little about how the epidemic actually affected people's daily lives.

Remarkably, modern bioarchaeological research has strongly vindicated Tuchman's intuition. Although the epidemic killed millions, no dramatic changes in skeletal indicators of health and lifestyle are directly ascribable to the epidemic. Most indicators either remained stable, or changed in response to other known historical trends. Traumatic though the plague was, it did not transform medieval people's health and lifeways radically.

Overall, the results suggest that there was much more continuity than change in medieval Cambridge — at least, in the living conditions that affected people's health and their skeletons. This agrees well with models that see the Black Death not as a single catastrophic event in isolation, but as part of an ongoing, general 14th–15th century crisis related to climatic worsening, overpopulation, new diseases, and other causes — a long-term process whose effects may be subtle, highly variable, and sometimes quite local.

This does not mean the Black Death was not genuinely catastrophic — it clearly was. But the chroniclers who wrote of universal death and societal collapse were not giving a representative picture of all communities at all times. The chronicler Matteo Villani described the Black Death as "a pestilence among men of every condition, age and sex," yet scientific analysis shows that even plague mortality followed patterns similar to normal medieval mortality, with age remaining a significant factor — suggesting the disaster, while devastating, was not as indiscriminate as contemporary accounts implied.

### 3. The Psychology of Negativity Bias

Tuchman's insight connects to well-established principles in psychology. Human beings are cognitively wired to attend to negative events far more than positive or neutral ones.

Media are frequently skewed toward the negative side when selecting news items. Framing research has empirically documented a negativity bias in several contexts, showing that negative framing exerts disproportionately strong effects on public perception and behaviour, as negative information carries more value compared to positive information.

The availability heuristic exacerbates the issue: repeated exposure to negative news makes adverse events feel disproportionately frequent and imminent. Moreover, confirmation bias ensures that individuals seek out distressing narratives that validate their preexisting anxieties. The cumulative effect of these biases is a distorted perception of global conditions, increasing public pessimism and fostering a sense of powerlessness.

The media's negativity bias significantly influences our perception of the world, as it tends to focus predominantly on bad news and negative events while disregarding positive ones. Consequently, this distorted perception leads us to believe that the world is more dangerous and chaotic than it truly is.

These modern findings validate precisely what Tuchman observed about the medieval record: the biases that distort our view of the present world are the same ones that shaped what was written down — and thus what historians read — about the past.

### 4. Survivorship Bias in Military and Institutional Contexts

The principle operates beyond historical narrative. A famous WWII example makes the point compellingly: early studies of damage inflicted on US bombers focused on the damage sustained by planes that made it back to their bases. The decision was made to reinforce the areas most often damaged by enemy fire. It was soon realised, however, that this was excluding the most important sources of data — the planes that never made it back to base. It became apparent that the most important places to reinforce the craft were where they had not been hit — because the planes that were hit there hadn't returned.

Historical accounts of war, plague, or famine share this structural problem: only the witnesses, survivors, and traumatised record-keepers survive to write. The majority who quietly lived through crises, adapted, and returned to routine lives left little trace.

---

## II. Qualifications and Challenges to Tuchman's Law

### 1. Some Disasters Genuinely Are Pervasive

While Tuchman's principle is broadly persuasive, one must be careful not to apply it so broadly that genuine catastrophes are minimised. The Black Death remains one of the most lethal events in human history. The assumption that the Black Death killed 25–33% of people in Western Europe between 1347–53 has long been accepted. The populations of some Italian cities, notably Florence, did not regain their pre-14th century size until the 19th century. These are not mere distortions of record-keeping
